Document [0]A Late Noachian to Early Hesperian age for the dichotomy is ruled out by the apparent Early Noachian age of the northern lowlands crust. Recent numerical modeling of early degree-1 mantle convection on Mars assumes a mantle layered in viscosity (Zhong & Zuber 2001, Zuber 2001), Zhong et al. 2004). For a viscosity contrast between the upper and lower mantle of at least 100, the predicted convection pattern results in preferential heating, upwelling, and crustal thinning in one hemisphere and downwelling and crustal thickening in the other hemisphere (Zhong & Zuber 2001, Zuber 2001), Roberts & Zhong 2006). In these models, layered viscosity allows a hemispheric convection pattern to organize at degree 1 rather than at shorter wavelengths, so the flow naturally produces a north-south style asymmetry in crustal structure. The modeling indicates that degree-1 mantle convection develops in timescales ranging from several hundred million years (Zhong & Zuber 2001), Zuber 2001) to on the order of 100 Myr (Roberts & Zhong 2006), depending on mantle viscosity. The smaller the viscosity, the faster the degree-1 mantle convection develops. For reasonable mantle viscosity for early Mars, degree-1 mantle convection can ensue in less than 100 Myr (Roberts & Zhong 2006), and is therefore consistent with an early origin for the dichotomy in early Martian geologic history. Widespread crustal extension (McGill & Dimitriou 1990) and volcanism (Zhong & Zuber 2001), Zuber 2001) in the northern lowlands likely accompanied the formation of the crustal dichotomy in this endogenic mantle-convection scenario.

The following observations for the Earth's mantle prompt us to focus on models for Mars in which the mantle viscosity increases with depth. (1) The viscosity in the asthenosphere may be 300 times smaller than that in the lower mantle, as inferred from studies of the Earth's geoid . The inferred viscosity contrast needs to be ∼600 if surface tectonic plates are considered in the geoid models . An even weaker asthenosphere is inferred from studies of earthquake cycles and postseismic rebound and remote triggering of earthquakes . (2) Observations of seismic anisotropy in the upper mantle (≤300 km in depth) and studies on silicate rheology suggest that mantle deformation at depths smaller than 200 to 300 km is controlled by dislocation creep , which can substantially weaken the flow with stress. A relatively weak shallow layer may also result from the depth dependence of homologous temperature and partial melting. The Rayleigh-Taylor instability analyses therefore suggest that viscosity stratification may be important for producing degree-1 mantle convection on Mars. We first present three cases to demonstrate the control of stratified viscosity on the development of degree-1 convection. All three cases have an 80-km thick high-viscosity lid, and their mantle viscosity structures are assumed to be time-invariant and dependent only on radius. Case 1 has an isoviscous mantle with a viscosity of 5×10^21 Pa s. The characteristic thermal structure for Case 1 has wavelengths comparable to the thickness of the mantle, consistent with previous studies and predictions from our Rayleigh-Taylor instability analysis for an isoviscous mantle . However, a global distribution of ejecta is supported by numerical studies, which suggest that the features related to the Borealis basin best match impacts of energies 3–6 1029 J and h = 45 degrees (Marinova et al., 2008). The present-day highland crustal thickness is relatively uniform and lacks crustal thickening near the edge of the Borealis basin, except for impact basins and the Tharsis region where the thicker crust is related to Tharsis volcanism (e.g., Zuber, 2001). This suggests that if the dichotomy was caused by the proposed giant impact, either crustal relaxation smoothed an initially diverse distribution of ejecta, or the initial ejecta distribution was relatively global and uniform. Subcircular lowlands such as Argyre, Chryse, Hellas, and Isidis Planitia and the plains south of Tharsis occupy previously recognized impact basins8–10. Document [0]Thermal evolution models suggest that the luminosities of both Uranus and Neptune are inconsistent with the classical assumption of an adiabatic interior. Such models commonly predict Uranus to be brighter and, recently, Neptune to be fainter than observed. In this work, we investigate the influence of a thermally conductive boundary layer on the evolution of Uranus- and Neptune-like planets. This thermal boundary layer (TBL) is assumed to be located deep in the planet and be caused by a steep compositional gradient between a H–He-dominated outer envelope and an ice-rich inner envelope. We investigate the effect of TBL thickness, thermal conductivity, and the time of TBL formation on the planet’s cooling behaviour. The calculations were performed with our recently developed tool based on the Henyey method for stellar evolution. We make use of state-of-the-art equations of state for hydrogen, helium, and water, as well as of thermal conductivity data for water calculated via ab initio methods. We find that even a thin conductive layer of a few kilometres has a significant influence on the planetary cooling. In our models, Uranus’ measured luminosity can only be reproduced if the planet has been near equilibrium with the solar incident flux for an extended period of time. For Neptune, we find a range of solutions with a near constant effective temperature at layer thicknesses of 15 km or larger, similar to Uranus. In addition, we find solutions for thin TBLs of a few km and strongly enhanced thermal conductivity. A ~ 1 Gyr later onset of the TBL reduces the present Δ*T* by an order of magnitude to only several 100 K. Our models suggest that a TBL can significantly influence the present planetary luminosity in both directions, making it appear either brighter or fainter than the adiabatic case. Key words: planets and satellites: physical evolution / planets and satellites: interiors / planets and satellites: individual: Uranus / planets and satellites: individual: Neptune
Document [1]We performed a suite of smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations to examine in detail what a giant impact would do to the young Uranus. The calculations follow the post-impact planet's internal structure, rotation rate, atmospheric retention, and the composition of material ejected into orbit, but their central result is how strongly the collision redistributes mass and energy inside the planet. Most of the material from the impactor's rocky core falls into the target's core. However, in higher-angular-momentum impacts, significant amounts of that rock become embedded anisotropically as lumps within the ice layer instead of reaching the center. Most of the impactor's ice and deposited energy end up in a hot, high-entropy shell at a radius of about 3 Earth radii, showing that the collision can move thermal energy outward rather than leaving it distributed as in an undisturbed planet. That post-impact structure provides a direct impact-based explanation for Uranus's observed lack of heat flow from the deep interior and may also matter for its asymmetric magnetic field. The simulations also recover an important dynamical requirement for this scenario: an impactor with a mass of at least 2 Earth masses can produce sufficiently rapid rotation in post-impact Uranus across a range of angular momenta. At least 90% of the atmosphere remains bound to the final planet after the collision, although 2 and 3 Earth-mass impactors can eject over half of the atmosphere beyond the Roche radius, with the strongest erosion for intermediate angular momenta around 3 x 10^36 kg m^2 s^-1. Rock is placed into orbit more efficiently by 2 Earth-mass impactors than by 3 Earth-mass ones because tidal disruption is suppressed for the more massive bodies. Taken together, these results support a giant impact as a physically plausible event that both tilted Uranus and redistributed interior material and energy in a way relevant to its low heat output.
Document [2]The simulation suite first shows that the post-impact rotation results are numerically stable. Median rotation periods for particles in the final planets vary little across the available numbers of particles, and the 2 Earth-mass impactor runs with velocities at infinity from 1 to 9 km s^-1 still bracket Uranus's present 17.24 hour rotation period. The general agreement with earlier work therefore tests differences in the colliding-body and material models more than numerical resolution itself. That agreement indicates the basic collision outcome is not a numerical artifact inherited from earlier low-resolution runs. The analysis then turns from rotation to the planet's interior, where the more relevant question is how a giant impact redistributes material inside the final planet rather than leaving Uranus close to its pre-impact state. Density profiles are decomposed by material type and by origin in the two colliding bodies for both relatively head-on and higher-angular-momentum impacts. Considering the suite in full, the summary plots show the destinations of impactor rock and impactor ice within the planet, with solid curves marking the rock that reaches the core and dashed curves the rock deposited elsewhere. The calculations track how much of the impactor's rock reaches the final core inside about 1.3 Earth radii and how much is deposited elsewhere in the planet, and they also track the radius at which the impactor's ice is deposited, with the spread shown as a 1-sigma percentile range. Those trends make clear that the collision does not simply add material to Uranus in a uniform way; it sorts rock and ice into different radial destinations depending on impactor mass and angular momentum. By identifying where the impactor's rock and ice end up inside Uranus, the simulations directly support the giant-impact explanation in which an early oblique collision reworked the planet's interior and changed how its internal heat remained stored or accessible afterward.

Document [4]We performed SPH simulations to test the idea that Uranus experienced a giant impact late in its formation and to trace the consequences of that collision for the post-impact planet. The atmosphere ejected by the impact usually comes from near the impact site, especially in the high-angular-momentum cases. For more head-on collisions, some atmosphere can also be lost from the opposite side of proto-Uranus because the icy mantle is driven outward so strongly. The simulations confirm the earlier result of S92 that the impactor must have a mass greater than 1 Earth mass to impart enough angular momentum to account for Uranus's present rotation, but the more relevant result here is where the impactor's mass and energy are deposited within the planet. Most of the impactor ice is delivered to the outer icy mantle, and the resulting redistribution depends strongly on impact geometry. Sub-adiabatic temperature gradients are produced toward the outer regions of the icy mantle, where most of that ice is deposited, and higher impact parameters can create a temperature inversion near the top of the ice layer. Those more-grazing collisions leave the impactor ice farther out, in a thin shell near the edge of the icy mantle, whereas more head-on impacts can implant substantial ice as much as roughly 0.5 Earth radii farther inward and less isotropically about the center. Higher-resolution runs also show strong inhomogeneities in the deposited impactor material and resolve the debris composition more clearly. The impactor's ice is distributed much more isotropically than its rocky core; most of the rock ends up near the top of the final core, some small chunks remain embedded in the icy mantle, and higher-angular-momentum impacts can even place significant amounts of rock and ice into orbit during tidal disruption. Altogether, the simulations show a giant impact redistributing Uranus's mass and energy in ways that could matter for the planet's weak present-day heat release.

Nonadiabatic models for Uranus's and Neptune's interiors and thermal evolution have recently been carried out (e.g., Nettelmann et al. 2016; Vazan & Helled 2020; Scheibe et al. 2021). Our results are still relevant to many of these models. The so-called thermal boundary layers at depth from Nettelmann et al. (2016) and Vazan & Helled (2020) place a separation between the outer envelope and deeper interior regions, with the envelope temperature referenced to a 1 bar equivalent temperature. Furthermore, the U-1 and U-2 models from Vazan & Helled (2020) also treat the outer envelope separately from deeper regions, with its temperature profile set using a 1 bar equivalent temperature. Although our results make no direct statement about the behavior of the deep interior of the planet, that interior may include extended regions of static stability that thermally isolate the deeper interior from the outer envelope, and our results still apply to the thermal evolution of these upper envelopes. Because Uranus and Neptune possess magnetic fields, some portions of their interiors need not be entirely nonconvective, but this does not preclude stable layers at depth, so any adiabatic description is probably relevant only for some fraction of the interior of Uranus and Neptune. The primary source of nonadiabatic behavior in the atmosphere is condensation, usually accounted for by the subadiabatic gradients caused by the latent heat of condensation. In Figure 5, we show the apparent effective temperature Te against the internal equivalent effective temperature Tint for various envelope condensate abundances. If convective inhibition does occur, it will largely cancel out the effect of moist adiabaticity. Therefore, using a dry adiabat to guess the 1 bar equivalent temperature is a better approximation than accounting for latent heat alone but neglecting convective inhibition.
Document [6]Uranus and Neptune, the so-called “ice giants”, are expected to contain significant amounts of icy materials by virtue of their distance from the Sun. The traditional models of the interior structure of Uranus and Neptune assume that the planets have a few layers: a compact core, an ice layer and a gas layer, with uniform composition in each one (see Figure 6). In these models, the heat transport in the layers is by convection, resulting in adiabatic interior structures. However, adiabatic models have difficulties explaining the observed luminosity of Uranus and, although less significantly, also of Neptune . This means that the interiors of the two planets cannot be described simply by a few uniform-composition layers with efficient convection throughout, and alternative models are required to explain the measurements. Such an alternative is a model with deep internal layering that suppresses convection and thermally isolates the deep interior from the outer envelope. Deep internal stratification in the ice giants has been suggested to explain the observed luminosity of Uranus , and of Neptune . Such a structure is also consistent with the complex magnetic fields of the two ice giants , as discussed in Section 2.4. Uranus may also have formed with an unusually small primordial heat reservoir and then cooled enough early on that little internal energy remained to radiate today. Yet, the current measurements of Uranus and Neptune are poor, and consequently, the observations cannot distinguish between the suggested models, and there is a great degeneracy in the extent of the deep stratified region and the planet's early thermal state. As of today, more observations are needed in order to achieve further progress in understanding the interiors of the two planets . The lack of accurate measurements and the coverage of the gas envelope make it hard to figure out what fractions of the ices and rocks are in the interiors of Uranus and Neptune . While observations of atmosphere-free Kuiper belt objects suggest an ice-to-rock ratio of 1: 2 , disk chemistry predicts a larger ice fraction in the locations of Uranus and Neptune .

Document [8]For 1 Earth-mass impactors, the delivered ice is deposited mostly on top of the pre-existing icy mantle regardless of angular momentum, because the projectile is not massive enough to disturb proto-Uranus very deeply. Larger projectiles behave differently. They inject impactor ice much farther into the final planet, especially in lower-angular-momentum, more head-on collisions, and those collisions also produce a somewhat thicker zone infiltrated by impactor ice than the higher-angular-momentum cases, which do not penetrate as significantly into the mantle and instead spread the delivered material into a thinner outer layer. The collision therefore does more than add mass: it also redistributes a significant amount of energy inside Uranus. Radial profiles of specific internal energy, extending to a little beyond the Roche radius and compared with the initial approximately adiabatic ice layer, show that in both low- and high-angular-momentum collisions the impactor rock that reaches the edge of the final core is much hotter than the largely undisturbed proto-Uranus rock. In the higher-angular-momentum cases, the delivered impactor ice creates a temperature inversion near the boundary between the ice and atmosphere, producing a hot, high-entropy outer layer. Lower-angular-momentum collisions likewise leave a sub-adiabatic energy gradient in the icy mantle, but over a broader range of radii because the impactor's mass and energy are deposited more deeply and less narrowly. Investigating the full implications of that departure from adiabatic behavior is beyond the scope of the paper, yet the profiles themselves show that the impact has thermally reorganized the planet. The important point is that the amount of energy added to Uranus and the radial location of that energy depend on the geometry and mass of the impactor. A giant collision can therefore rearrange where internal heat is stored and how accessible it is, rather than leaving Uranus with the thermal structure of an undisturbed cooling planet.
Document [9]Across the simulation suite, the destination of the impactor's material depends strongly on collision geometry, showing that a giant impact can leave Uranus with a markedly redistributed interior. Relatively head-on collisions deliver practically all of the impactor's rock to the core. As angular momentum increases, however, a growing fraction of that rock is deposited higher in the planet's ice layer or is even placed into orbit, and some initially grazing encounters are followed by a much more head-on secondary collision of the core after the impactor's ice has been stripped and some angular momentum has been lost. For sufficiently high-angular-momentum collisions, as much as 40% of the rock in 2 and 3 Earth-mass impactors remains embedded in the icy mantle instead of reaching the core. In the simulations, that material survives as well-resolved, mostly spherical lumps rather than being mixed uniformly through the planet, and the rock added during the collision is not distributed isotropically with respect to the center. For 2 Earth-mass impactors, 90% of the delivered rock covers only about 50% of the full 4 pi steradians seen from the planet's center, and for 3 Earth-mass impactors the coverage rises only to about 70%. The deposited ice is usually more isotropic than the rock, except in head-on impacts, where 90% of the delivered ice still subtends only about 40% of 4 pi steradians. The exact radial destinations of that impactor ice matter because where it is deposited may have profound implications for Uranus's internal structure and heat flow. Because a giant impact can leave both rock and ice concentrated at specific depths and directions rather than smoothly mixed, the event offers a concrete way to restructure Uranus internally and alter how effectively its interior heat reaches the surface.

This study introduces a novel structural analysis of the Indus script (c. 3300-1900 BCE) to determine if it represents a full linguistic writing system. Unlike previous methods, this research focuses on the inherent structural properties of over 400 Indus signs to quantify the primary constituent signs. Through a new grid-based decomposition, compound signs were visually dissected, consistent diacritics identified, and sign formation principles clarified. This rigorous examination revealed a set of fundamental signs, suggesting an underlying system despite stylistic variations in sign formation, composition, and combination. This finding supports the hypothesis that the Indus inscriptions encode language. Furthermore, the study proposes preliminary phonetic assignments, offering a tentative reading of Indus texts to support the proposed decipherment. On that basis, the article argues that "piru"-based words for ivory likely originated in the IVC, since the ancient Egyptian words used for African ivory, such as "ab", "abu", "āb", beḥu, and "netcheḥ-t", have no phonetic connection to "piru". Their spread into the languages of distant countries is therefore attributed to the ancient ivory trade, whose Asian branch the article associates strongly with IVC traders. The same method is then extended beyond ivory. By studying literary evidence and analysing common substrate words for traded commodities that show similar roots across a wide range of otherwise different languages, the article seeks the names of other widely travelled goods that should have originated in the IVC. It then tries to connect those nouns to Indus signs because, in this account, the trade- and tax-related records conveyed through the inscriptions must have contained names of certain ancient commodities. Methodologically, the paragraph therefore treats the inscriptions as a narrowly bounded administrative-commercial record system encoding commodity terms within exchange and taxation, rather than as an open-ended corpus with unrestricted subject matter. Because the semantic analysis moves sign by sign through several layers of archaeological, linguistic, historical, and script-internal evidence, the paragraph presents the commodity identifications as part of a focused inquiry into that limited commercial domain. The goal is not to recover every possible topic of expression, but to identify the small set of goods and fiscal categories that would have mattered most in routine administrative handling.

Finding fire: Testing the opportunistic / ‘low fire’ model We have highlighted the key challenges to understanding the use of fire in the European Lower Palaeolithic record: 1) The amount of fire evidence and the location(s) of that evidence; 2) The fire use behaviours this evidence represents; and 3) The related question of fire function. Based on the evidence described in Sections 4 and 5, we tentatively propose that our opportunistic, or ‘low fire’, model is supported by the currently known archaeological record. To further test the ‘low fire’ model, a truly holistic approach is required. This should include experimental work, experiential observations, and cost-benefit analysis of the ‘micro-scale’ factors such as fuel provisioning (e.g., Henry et al., 2018), alongside further understanding of the wider archaeological and environmental context (the ‘macro-scale’ issues). We have shown that not only is the amount of evidence for fire use in the Lower Palaeolithic record of temperate regions limited to a very small number of sites (e.g., Beeches Pit, Menez-Dregan, Bilzingsleben and Vértesszőlős in central and north-western Europe; Table 2), but the location of these sites is focused on springs and rock shelters. The limited range of landscape settings represented by those sites in comparison to the wider archaeological record suggests either a) fire use was only taking place in selected locations within the landscape, or b) these landscape locations are those where fire is more likely to be preserved. Most plausible is a combination of both a) and b), consistent with opportunistic access to naturally available fire.

However, there may well be a bias here in our evidence from Africa. In the first place, most of the early African sites are ephemeral open-air ones, where charcoal and ash could easily have been blown away, unlike the caves that dominate the evidence from Eurasia. Secondly, there are now very few African Middle Pleistocene sites, as ones such as Olorgesailie and Kilombe have been redated to the late Lower Pleistocene. (Gowlett asks, What important African sites can be placed with certainty in the period 700, 000-300, 000 years ago?) The absence of pertinent data from African Middle Pleistocene sites may therefore indicate an absence of early- to mid-Middle Pleistocene sites and not just an absence of sites with the right preservational contexts. To some extent, imitation will be a possible starting point for a quicker learning of the causal traits of the collected material. Hence, if teaching by communicating concepts and relations between concepts (SOM table 2) are exploited, the learning can become more efficient. For example, learning concepts for materials will help finding suitable wood and how long it will burn. Another example is learning which properties signal dryness will also make the selection of material more efficient. A further cognitive factor is knowledge about where appropriate material can be found, for example, on which types of trees the best fungus for tinder grows. Adler1 The use of fre played an important role in the social and technological development of the genus Homo. Most archaeologists agree that this was a multi-stage process, beginning with the exploitation of natural fres and ending with the ability to create fre from scratch. Some have argued that in the Middle Palaeolithic (MP) hominin fre use was limited by the availability of fre in the landscape. Here, we present a record of the abundance of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), organic compounds that are produced during the combustion of organic material, from Lusakert Cave, a MP site in Armenia. We fnd no correlation between the abundance of light PAHs (3–4 rings), which are a major component of wildfre PAH emissions and are shown to disperse widely during fre events, and heavy PAHs (5–6 rings), which are a major component of particulate emissions of burned wood. Instead, we fnd heavy PAHs correlate with MP artifact density at the site. Given that hPAH abundance correlates with occupation intensity rather than lPAH abundance, we argue that MP hominins were able to control fre and utilize it regardless of the variability of fres in the environment. Together with other studies on MP fre use, these results suggest that the ability of hominins to manipulate fre independent of exploitation of wildfres was spatially variable in the MP and may have developed multiple times in the genus Homo. Te use of fre played a key role in the evolution of the genus Homo1 , allowing for warmth, cooking, birch tar production, protection from predators, a venue for social interactions and access to high latitudes and dark caves2 . Evidence of hominin fre use is present in the archaeological record beginning around 1.5 million years ago3–5 , and while it has long been assumed that a variety of hominin species could use fre5–7 , the degree to which hominins were able to intentionally create and control fre (pyrotechnology) is debated8–17.
Document [9]The process of making fire requires two fire sticks, called male and female, and a bunch of woolly grass or tinder. The male stick, held vertically, is twirled rapidly in a small notch in the female stick, which is placed horizontally on the ground [held steady by pressing a foot on one end], till the fine wood dust produced by the twirling is ignited by friction. The smouldering wood dust is quickly tipped into the bunch of grass, which is picked up and gently blown till the grass bursts into flame. The grass is then placed on the ground. Small twigs ready at hand are placed on the grass for kindling, and as soon as they are ignited pieces of wood are added. The male stick is usually made of a hard wood, the female stick of a soft wood [with a notch cut into it]. The male stick must fit into the notch exactly. [. . .] Frequently two men make fire together. As one pair of hands reaches the bottom of the stick, the second pair is ready at the top to keep the twirling continuous. Our exploration into the cognition of firemaking is part of a long-term project wherein we apply theoretical frameworks for causal and social cognition to the analysis of different evolutionary problems. Here we add prospective cognition and rehearsal. These frameworks have been published previously, so we do not discuss them here, but provide tabulated summaries and definitions in the supporting online material (SOM) for easy reference. In short, a basic question for a theory of causal cognition is what kind of entities can serve as causes. One can distinguish between agent causes (when some animate being exerts a force), natural causes (physical/chemical/biological causes where natural phenomena generate forces) and mental causes (psychological/social causes, where mental phenomena function as causes). It is widely thought that causal cognition underpins technical reasoning (McCormack et al. 2011; Osiurak et al. 2020).

The gas flow was subsequently switched to CO, during which the XAS spectra were recorded to monitor the structural evolution during the oxidative disruption of Rh species. A similar pre-treatment procedure was also adopted before in situ XAS measurement, which was then performed after exposure to pressurized gas of H2/CO/propene/Ar (4 MPa, 47: 47: 2: 4, v/v/v/v) at 90 °C. A library containing varieties of models as a statistical foundation for the extraction of Rh–Rh, Rh–O and Rh–C scattering paths was first established. In particular, the Rh–Rh scattering path was extracted from the crystal structure of Rh metal and Rh6(CO)16. Rh metal is the most commonly used standard and Rh6(CO)16 is a thermodynamically stable organometallic compound with Rh cluster size comparable with our case. The Rh–O scattering path was extracted from the crystal structure of Rh2O3 and a theoretical [Rh(CO)2]@MEL model optimized from DFT calculations. Rh2O3 is the most frequently used Rh oxide standard. The [Rh(CO)2]@MEL model with direct Rh–O bonding to zeolite should be more representative of the catalyst. Document [1]However, based on the literature several common crucial requirements for a homogeneous Rh hydroformylation catalyst can be summarized: - The catalytically active species is an in-situ formed unsaturated 16e- Rh hydride complex - At least one CO ligand must be present within the catalytically active Rh complex - The coordination number around the Rh center alters between 4 and 6 within the catalytic cycle - A change in oxidation state of the Rh center from +I to +III (and back to +I) occurs during the catalytic cycle With the aim to combine the activity and selectivity of molecular hydroformylation catalysts and the advantages in terms of catalyst stability and eased recovery, research has been directed towards heterogenized rhodium hydroformylation catalysts. We developed a scheme to group the different efforts made which is summarized in Figure 5. The attempts can be roughly divided into the deposition of molecular rhodium complexes or metallic rhodium nanoparticles on a solid support. The first reports tackling the heterogenization of catalysts with respect to hydroformylation reactions included the deposition of molecular rhodium complexes, such as metal carbonyl complexes, on solid support materials. This approach has been reviewed perfectly by Lenarda et al. in 1996, showing the progresses made in this field and the challenges that have been encountered, such as the low catalytic activity of the materials and the leaching of Rh, especially when applied in liquid phase catalysis . In subsequent publications also the deposition of metallic nanoparticles and modified metallic nanoparticles on solid supports such as zeolites has been investigated. In these zeolite-supported nanoparticle formulations, the active sites for propene hydroformylation are Rh nanoparticles whose coordinatively unsaturated edge sites perform the catalytic cycle. Although the supported metal nanoparticles do not show leaching of Rh only low activities and selectivities have been achieved.

question: Which kinetic mechanisms or non-ideal terms in the generalized Ohm's law are responsible for the breaking and dissipation of magnetic field lines within the electron diffusion region of collisionless reconnection?
perspectives: Nongyrotropic electron pressure-tensor divergence
Electron inertia in the electron momentum equation
Anomalous resistivity from wave-particle scattering
context:
Document [0]Within the electron diffusion region, where L < ρe, the weak-gradient assumptions underlying electron adiabaticity are not realized, so simple moment-based diagnostics are insufficient. A common misconception is that conservation or violation of the electron magnetic moment can be ascertained by monitoring the constancy of a moment quantity such as kTe/B, which has the same units as μe. However, it is easy to construct Vlasov solutions that conserve μ for every particle but do not conserve the related moment quantity (Scudder et al. 1986). Thus, variability of kTe/B need not by itself establish the relevant electron behavior. The key signature relevant to the divergence of a nongyrotropic electron pressure tensor is that the electron probability distribution in the proper frame, fe(w), depends intrinsically on all three polar variables, where w = v - Ue is the electron velocity relative to the electron bulk velocity, Ue. Making observations that can discern this behavior requires simultaneous sampling of all octants of velocity space; measurements that use spacecraft rotation to build up the gyrophase distribution of the 3-D velocity distribution are invariably aliased against detecting these signatures. In addition, defensible determinations of Ue in the presence of UV, photoelectrons, spacecraft charging, and time aliasing of data acquisition are a necessary experimental prerequisite for detecting these expected gyrophase dependences within the electron diffusion region.
Document [1]Apart from this feature, the electrons in the EDR express non-gyrotropic electron distributions in the plane perpendicular to the magnetic field, especially close to the center reconnection site (Ng et al. 2011; Scudder et al. 2012; Swisdak 2016). This phenomenon is also associated with electron acceleration in the EDR (Huang et al. 2012a; Oka et al. 2016) and forms a crescent shape in the electron distribution function (Fig. 6; Hesse et al. 2014). These signatures are further discussed in Sect. 3. Besides, the nongyrotropic electron pressure tensor is the crucial source for balancing the non-ideal electric field in terms of the generalized Ohm’s law, especially the Y component, and for sustaining the localized regime at the inflow edge of the EDR (Egedal et al. 2013).
Document [2]One of the recurring problems in magnetic reconnection is the identification of the appropriate generalized Ohm's law. In weakly collisional plasmas with a strong magnetic guide field component, a fluid model may be adopted in which electron inertia is the term that permits field lines to break in the absence of collisions. The emphasis is on collisionless field-line breaking by electron inertia itself. This inertial breaking of flux freezing is central to the structure of the reconnection region and is consistent with the fast relaxation times of sawtooth oscillations in tokamak plasmas. The possibility of nonlinear, irreversible magnetic reconnection without ordinary dissipation is therefore addressed in a framework where electron inertia remains the key non-ideal ingredient. In this collisionless picture, magnetic islands can grow and reach a saturated state in a coarse-grained sense, while magnetic energy is transferred to kinetic energy at progressively smaller spatial scales through phase mixing. The same model is then applied to driven reconnection events near a magnetic X-line observed in the VTF experiment at MIT. There the reconnection is driven by externally induced plasma flows in a background magnetic configuration with a hyperbolic null in the reconnection plane and a magnetic guide field component perpendicular to that plane. In the limit of a strong guide field and a sufficiently weak external drive for a linear approximation to hold, the evolution does not reach a stationary state. Instead, the reconnection process develops in two phases: an initial phase with a rate that is a fraction of the Alfvén frequency, and a later phase whose rate is determined by the electron collision frequency.
Document [3]The electron physics in the collisionless magnetic reconnection is studied using data from the Polar spacecraft. Among the types of discontinuities in space plasmas, the Electron Diffusion Region (EDR) at the center of the reconnection has the theoretically unique properties that its thickness is of order of the electron gyroradius, and in such a region electrons are demagnetized with a non-gyrotropic pressure tensor. These unusual properties of EDRs reflect the expected violation of guiding center theory for electrons and are exploited in this thesis. We use four dimensionless, diagnostic, single spacecraft observables derived from theoretical properties of EDRs to locate them. They are electron agyrotropy, out-of-interconnection-plane electron Mach number, and dimensionless thresholds for electric field strengths parallel and perpendicular to the magnetic field. These observables are constructible using the electron density, bulk velocity, pressure tensor, and the electromagnetic field data. With a 3-year survey using particle data from a slower version of Hydra’s moment producing system, M3, the vast preponderance of these dimensionless parameters are below unity, which is consistent with the theoretical expectations for most space plasmas being strongly magnetized. The unusual outliers with the demagnetization parameters over unity (< 1%) in the distribution are geophysically distributed near the magnetopause within 8-9Re shells and collected as potential reconnection sites, although a number of other possibilities are also considered in this thesis such as data processing anomalies, systematic effects of data acquisition and aliasing. It is shown that plasma particle data with the highest time resolution possible are needed to improve the time aliasing issues, and to sense the rapidly changing and short scale current structure like the EDR. We use a recently developed algorithm G3/T1, which reduces the aliasing time of the 3D analysis of products of the Polar Hydra Hot Plasma Analyzer by a factor of 12. With this new technique, we have found that among these outliers some demagnetization signatures are ameliorated by higher time cadences and the ones caused by time aliasing effects are ruled out.
Document [4]If at all, contribution will come only from the electron pressure term Pe which, in the center of the current layer, may develop non-diagonal elements. The latter, in particular, have been attributed to be important drivers of reconnection (cf. e.g., , and references to earlier papers of the same authors therein). In collisionless plasmas such non-diagonal pressure tensor elements can arise in the current sheet and are therefore of interest in the electron diffusion region. Non-diagonal pressure tensor elements enter the electron-fluid description through the pressure tensor and can affect the short electron scales relevant for collisionless reconnection. It is, however, not completely clear whether non-diagonal pressure terms based on physical effects will indeed be generated at a reconnection site. Wave-particle scattering by microinstabilities can produce anomalous resistivity, which dissipates electron current and helps violate the frozen-in condition in the diffusion region. The opinions are ambiguous on this matter. Numerical particle-in-cell simulations do indicate that it is indeed the pressure tensor effect which takes responsibility for collisionless reconnection. Related work also noted that the case is a bit obscured by the imprecise definition of the main axes of the pressure tensor near a reconnection site.
Document [5]When (E + v × B)M > 0, the magnetic flux is transported downstream faster than the plasma, meaning the magnetic field slips through or diffuses across the plasma. When (E + v × B)M < 0, the particles are instead outrunning, or catching up with, the field. These criteria are used to distinguish inner and outer diffusion regions, because they directly diagnose the relative motion between plasma and field in the non-ideal region. Any such non-ideal electric field must satisfy momentum balance, and that balance is generally written through the generalized Ohm's law. In the tenuous plasma considered here, the classical Spitzer form R = ηJ is negligible, so ordinary collisions do not provide the conductivity that would support the current. The simple resistive expression is still instructive, however, because it makes clear that the non-ideal electric field has to be sustained by some process that regulates the current density, or inversely that a finite conductivity, σ = 1/η, must exist to permit a finite current J = σR. Speiser showed that electron inertia can provide exactly this role when one takes into account the finite dwell time of particles in the diffusion region. The point is not that the current becomes collisional, but that the classical collisional time scale is replaced by a finite residence time inside the diffusion region. That residence time is long enough for the reconnection electric field to accelerate electrons, yet finite enough to limit how much momentum can be accumulated in the current sheet there locally in that layer. The acceleration by the reconnection electric field that drives the reconnection current is therefore limited by this finite dwell time. Because the dwell time is set by the topology of reconnection itself, electron inertia supplies an effective conductivity proportional to the reconnection electric field. In that sense, the finite current and the slippage of magnetic flux relative to the plasma are sustained by inertial physics rather than by classical resistivity.
Document [6]These quantities are useful in mapping the dissipation region both in measurements as in simulations thus identifying the physical reconnection site. Observations support this measure in symmetric reconnection settings like in the magnetotail. In non-symmetric reconnection, however, the measure seems not as useful, as has been discussed by Pritchett . The time dependent inertial term can be expressed as Einert ≈ σ−1inertJ through the “inertial conductivity” σinert = 0ω2e τinert. The time τinert is the time of change of the current. This time is usually long compared with the period of plasma oscillations. In the magnetotail with density N ∼ 106 m−3 one has σinert ≈ 5 × 10−3τinert S. Therefore, moderately fast current oscillations could well contribute to inertial resistivity providing sufficient inertial diffusivity for reconnection. Document [7]A review of the present status of the theory of magnetic reconnection is given. First the basic concepts are introduced, including the MHD equations, the generalized Ohm's law, and the conservation laws. After contrasting this with strongly collisional plasmas, where reconnection proceeds through resistive current sheets, the weakly collisional limit is described for low-β plasmas in which the departure from ideal behavior is governed by electron inertia. In this presentation, weak-collisionality reconnection is treated as a nondissipative problem rather than a resistive one. The equations of electron magnetohydrodynamics are introduced as the framework for analyzing this configuration, yielding reconnection rates that are independent of the smallness parameters of the system. Within this collisionless treatment, electron inertia is the non-ideal ingredient that enables rapid reconnection. Hence collisionless reconnection can proceed very rapidly, essentially on the Alfvén time scale.

question: Which surface conditions or interfacial layers are responsible for the exceptionally low friction observed when tetrahedral amorphous carbon slides within unsaturated oxygenated lubricants or glycerol?
perspectives: A graphene-like sp2-rich carbon tribolayer formed during rubbing
A hydroxyl-terminated passivated carbon surface with minimal interfacial adhesion
A tribochemically generated oxygen-containing polymeric boundary layer
context:
Document [0]For the study of the microstructure and properties of DLC, there are mainly three types of research methods: density functional theory (DFT) simulation based on quantum mechanics, first-principles calculation based on classical mechanics, and MD simulation based on classical mechanics. Some good progress has been made among these methods. MD is a set of molecular simulation methods that mainly rely on Newtonian mechanics to simulate the motion of molecular systems, extract samples from systems composed of different states of molecular systems, and calculate the integral configuration of the system. MD can be used to calculate the thermodynamic properties and other macroscopic properties of the system based on the results of the integral configuration. MD studies atoms or groups of atoms, and the system size is relatively large compared to DFT calculations. The bond length and bond angle between molecules are determined by the force field, making it difficult to carry out detailed research. MD is mostly used for large molecular systems and is often used in conjunction with DFT calculations when studying microproperties, mainly for the construction of DLC models. Through the MD modeling of DLC films, it has been found that the super-slip properties of DLC are closely related to the structural evolution of the sliding interface . For a-C or Ta-C films, the molecular modeling design of the friction process simulates interfacial sliding by adjusting the steady-state velocity. This aims to explain the formation of graphitized and carbon-rich interfacial layers during rubbing, as shown in Figure 7 . The results show that graphene-like carbon features can be observed at the sliding interface. The interfacial bonding is weakened, which favors easier shear. Overall, the interface becomes enriched in graphitized, sp2-rich carbon during friction, including for ta-C sliding in glycerol or other unsaturated oxygenated lubricants.
Document [1]When the tribo-couples are changed, the tribology behavior of a-C: H film changes accordingly, as shown in Figure 8. Mechanical action should also play an important role in the superlubricity of a-C: H films in a vacuum . Compared with Al2O3 balls, ZrO2, Si3N4, and SiC balls show stronger interactions with the diamond surface, and the higher hardness and contact stress of SiC balls can lead to more severe wear of the a-C: H film, thereby reducing the durability of superlubricity. In related simulations using surface-doped a-C models with materials such as diamond or methanol, the friction force was approximately zero . Through calculation, it was found that an ultra-thin graphene-like friction layer was formed on the friction interface, and the specific formation reason was shear localization rather than uniform deformation. The main manifestation is the redirection (orientation angle 90%) of C-C covalent bonds that occur preferentially in the friction contact area, producing a structurally ordered graphene-like friction layer.
Document [2]This is because rubbing reconstructs the contact surface, resulting in the structure of the transfer film being mainly composed of sp2-C . Other carbon-based amorphous films also exhibit extremely low μ. The μ can reach 0.01, and the wear rate can also be extremely low at 6.41 × 10−18 mm3/Nm. During the friction process, the contact evolves toward an amorphous interfacial layer. In situ this generates an interface transfer film enriched in graphitized carbon, thereby achieving ultra-low friction–wear and greatly reducing energy loss . A transfer film is also generated in situ on the friction-sliding surface induced by friction. The composition of the transfer film includes hexagonal graphene-like carbon rings caused by the thermal and strain effects of repeated friction. These ring-shaped carbon structures form a stable sp2-rich tribolayer, thereby achieving ultra-low friction and wear in the atmospheric environment. At the sliding interface, excellent lubrication effects can also be achieved as the transfer film develops during rubbing. The structure of the transfer film can include oxygen-containing species together with a more ordered sp2-C phase. With unsaturated oxygenated lubricants, the sliding contact can likewise tribochemically generate an oxygen-containing polymeric boundary layer on tetrahedral amorphous carbon, and this interfacial film underlies the superlow friction. Additionally, continued rubbing participates in the formation of a lubricating transfer film .
Document [3]Under the action of a frictional force, the hydrogen concentration and methane gas emission in the transfer film structure are high, and this interface emission induces DLC atomic-level chemical wear. With the increase in hydrogen concentration in a-C: H, chemical wear and mechanical wear increase and decrease, respectively. Total wear shows a concave hydrogen concentration dependence, with an optimal hydrogen concentration of about 20% . Injecting low-temperature nitrogen into the ultra-high vacuum environment, DLC’s μ can be further reduced to 0.003, with the wear rate of almost zero (4.6 × 10−10 mm3/Nm), as shown in Table 1. A graphitized structure was also found in its transfer film structure, together with a local friction-induced increase in the content of sp2-C bonds (Figure 5), thereby achieving ultra-low friction and wear of the hard carbon film. The formation and persistence of this smooth graphitized tribolayer on the wear track are associated with long-lasting superlubrication.
Document [4]Besides the DLC systems already discussed, diamond has attracted special attention for its potential superlubricity. From a tribological standpoint, bulk diamond or thin diamond films combine extreme hardness, rigidity, and wear resistance, but the friction that they exhibit is strongly affected by the gaseous species present in the surrounding atmosphere. The paragraph specifically identifies hydrogen, oxygen, and water molecules as species that can alter diamond friction by changing the chemistry at the sliding interface. Recent studies by Kumar et al. and Konicek et al. confirmed extraordinary wear resistance of ultrananocrystalline diamond films and also reported ultralow friction, down to about 0.01 or below at the macroscale, when sliding occurred in humid air. The explanation offered for those results is a passivation mechanism operating directly on the carbon surface. Water molecules reaching the sliding contact were argued to dissociate into hydrogen and hydroxyl ions. Those reaction products then effectively passivated the dangling sigma bonds of the surface diamond atoms at the contact interface. Once those otherwise reactive bonds were saturated, the surfaces were less able to form strong adhesive carbon-carbon junctions across the interface, so sliding resistance dropped while the inherent wear resistance of diamond was retained. This means that the same hard carbon surface can shift toward ultralow friction when the atmosphere continuously supplies water that can dissociate and terminate reactive sites at the contact. The resulting change is localized at the topmost carbon atoms that control adhesion, rather than in the bulk mechanical properties of the film. In humid air, the H and OH species produced at the interface cap dangling sigma bonds, reduce interfacial reactivity, and suppress the adhesion that would otherwise raise friction during sliding. Because the substrate remains diamond, the system preserves its high load-bearing capacity and wear resistance even while the interface becomes easier to shear. The paragraph therefore points to a humid, water-fed interfacial state in which hydroxyl- and hydrogen-terminated surface sites suppress adhesion and produce ultralow interfacial shear on carbon. That is the key low-friction condition emphasized here.
Document [5]The structures of sp2-rich carbon films could predetermine interfacial transformation routes and resulting products. GLC with a thickness of 500 nm was prepared on steel substrates and balls by DC-pulsed plasma chemical-vapor deposition (PECVD). Sp2-rich clusters can grow in size by forming "regular graphene" stacks (3–5 nm) possessing a layered structure like graphite. In conclusion, during sliding the GLC is converted, relative to the initial 3–5 nm "regular graphene" stacks, into larger and more ordered graphene by adaptively sliding-oriented rehybridization and rearrangement along the sliding direction. With this conversion, super-low friction is realized by the low-shear strength of the larger, more ordered graphene tribolayer formed at the interface.
Document [6]Finally, a transfer film composed of curved multilayer graphene strips is formed in situ on the frictional sliding contact surface. In a dry inert environment, non-doped amorphous carbon films create graphitized transfer films on the contact surface. These transfer films produce macroscopic super-slip effects. Even when the films are doped with other elements, their transfer film structures still contain graphitized structures generated by friction-induced processes. Under harsh environments, friction can also induce re-hybridization from sp3-C to sp2-C at the sliding interface. The resulting graphitized transfer film and friction-induced augmentation of the sp2 bond content in certain locations increase the smoothness of the sliding interface, induce weak interactions between the friction interfaces, and have a positive effect on the ultra-low friction and wear of hard carbon films.
Document [7]From an experimental and application point of view, researchers must be mindful that water can enter tribosystems over time and strongly influence measured friction behavior. The paragraph first notes that in nanocrystalline MoS2, ambient water contamination of stored samples is significant and that physically adsorbed structural water can be removed much more rapidly by thermal treatment than by vacuum desorption. That contrast matters because the effect of water on carbonaceous lubricants is essentially opposite. For bulk diamonds, diamond thin films, ultra-nanocrystalline diamonds, diamond-like carbon, and tetrahedral amorphous carbon thin films, achieving and maintaining low friction and wear required surface passivation of the reactive carbon surface. In these systems, water, hydrogen and the OH groups supplied by glycerol were suggested as favorable molecules for passivating dangling sigma bonds or other unsaturated covalent bonds. Konicek et al. then showed lower friction across different normal loads as relative humidity increased for UNCD and ta-C thin films, which is consistent with humid environments supplying passivating species to the interface. The mechanistic statement in the paragraph is that passivation with H, OH, or related groups hinders the formation of strong covalent bonds across self-mating carbon interfaces. The adsorbed species therefore do more than cap dangling sigma bonds: they also weaken pi-pi interactions between carbon atoms on the counterfaces, further enhancing superlubricity. As an engineering strategy, the window for superlubricity in DLC and ta-C, whether in self-mating contacts or against steel, can therefore be broadened by deliberately introducing adsorbates that strengthen this hydrophilic, passivated interfacial state. question: Which processes are responsible for the occurrence of seismic events at depths exceeding 300 km?
perspectives: Transformational faulting in metastable olivine
Dehydration embrittlement of hydrous minerals carried to depth
Thermal runaway shear instability in an adiabatically heated fault zone

Document [0]The activity of deep-focus earthquakes, which increases with depth from ~400 km to a peak at ~6oo km, is enigmatic, because conventional brittle failure is unlikely to occur at elevated pressures. It becomes increasingly clear that pressure-induced phase transitions of olivine are responsible for the occurrence of the earthquakes, based on deformation experiments under pressure. However, many such experiments were made using analogue materials and those on mantle olivine are required to verify the hypotheses developed by these studies. Here we report the results of deformation experiments on (Mg, Fe)SiO4 olivine at l1-17 GPa and 860-1350 K, equivalent to the conditions of the slabs subducted into the mantle transition zone. We find that throughgoing faulting occurs only at very limited temperatures of 1100-l160 K, accompanied by intense acoustic emissions at the onset of rupture. Faulting occurs along a weak layer, which is formed via linking-up of lenticular packets filled with nanocrystalline olivine and wadsleyite. Our study suggests that transformational faulting occurs on the isothermal surface of the metastable olivine wedge in slabs, leading to deep-focus earthquakes in limited regions and depth range. (Mg, Fe)SiO4 olivine is the major mineral in the Earth's mantle and subducting slabs; it shows successive phase transitions to wadsleyite (at pressures around 13 GPa) and ringwoodite (-20 GPa) with modified spinel and spinel structures, respectively. Olivine decomposes into an assemblage of bridgmanite + ferro-periclase (-24 GPa) with increasing pressure, although the transitions may proceed via an intermediate spinelloid structurel. An increase in the frequency of earthquakes at depths from ~400 km to -600 km² seems to be linked to the phase transitions of olivine. An abrupt decrease in the seismicity from a peak at ~600 km to almost zero at 680 km², with a very limited number of earthquakes at deeper regions down to 750 km³, also implies an essential role of the phase transitions of olivine on occurrence of deepfocus earthquakes. The concept of transformational faulting upon the phase transitions of olivine, which is triggered by propagation and linking-up of lens-shaped 'anticracks', has been widely proposed to explain faulting in the mantle transition zone (410 - 660 km in depth), based on experimental studies on a germanate analogue (MgzGeO4)4.5 and ice6. The anticrack is orientated normal to the direction of the maximum compressive stress and is filled with a nanocrystalline aggregate of the high-pressure phases, that behaves as a low-viscosity layer due to grain-size-sensitive (GSS) creep457.

Consequently, the legacy effects of fire that operate on the longest timescales are systematically excluded from models of the carbon cycle and from global carbon budgets.

Investigators often posit that pyrophilic taxa possess traits that help them launch ecological succession after fire. These include stress tolerance to ultraviolet exposure, heavy metals, elevated pH and/or high heat, the ability to degrade pyrolysed carbon, and rapid growth rates marked by high rRNA copy numbers22, 80, 84. Net ecosystem carbon uptake represents the balance of photosynthesis to respiration and determines whether an ecosystem is a carbon sink or source. Carbon sinks develop when more carbon is taken up through photosynthesis and stored in biomass than is released through plant and microbial respiration. Given that wildfire disturbance can reduce photosynthesis on timescales from years to decades86 and has variable effects on ecosystem respiration87, 88, it is therefore critical to track carbon pools and fluxes over time and with variability in local climate conditions and fire severity87, 89. Within that broader accounting, microbial communities that can degrade pyrolysed carbon and are associated with mineralization pathways support a trajectory in which fire-derived carbon is actively turned over rather than simply persisting in place.
